idiom_name: closure-scoped strategy: OSAllocatedUnfairLock.withLock / Synchronization.Mutex.withLock (actors as the isolation alternative)
implementation_notes: Swift's modern locks are closure-scoped strategy objects: OSAllocatedUnfairLock (iOS 16/macOS 13) and Synchronization.Mutex (iOS 18/macOS 15) both expose withLock(_:), which acquires, runs the closure and releases - Scoped Locking as an API rather than a guard class - while NSLock/NSRecursiveLock remain the Foundation fallback and actors (Swift 5.5+) are the language's own answer for state that can simply be isolated. A component can hold whichever strategy it was given, but the idiomatic choice is to make it an actor and not lock at all; keep the lock-based strategy for code that must stay synchronous, cannot await, or must be callable from non-concurrent contexts. Both modern types are Sendable value-like handles, so the policy can be injected without the reference-sharing caveats of NSLock.
pitfalls: OSAllocatedUnfairLock and Synchronization.Mutex are not re-entrant: calling withLock from inside a critical section deadlocks, and an actor cannot substitute for a lock in a synchronous function that must not await.
The closure must not suspend - awaiting inside withLock holds the lock across a suspension, which the synchronous API cannot express and which surfaces only under contention.
NSLock/NSRecursiveLock are reference types: a struct that copies one shares the same lock, so value semantics give no protection when two components end up locking each other's state.
